title: Isomerism
examples: What is the difference between structural and geometric isomers?
How do I know if two molecules are isomers?
Can you show me an example of an E/Z isomer?

explain.say: Today we explore isomerism in organic chemistry.

items: Isomers have the same molecular formula.
They have different arrangements of atoms.
This difference causes different chemical properties.

explain.say: Geometric isomers are a type of structural isomer.
We use E and Z to describe geometric isomers.

faq.q: What is the main difference between structural and geometric isomers?
faq.a: Structural isomers have different connectivity of atoms. Geometric isomers are a specific type of structural isomer involving restricted rotation around a double bond.
asks: Are they always related to double bonds?
How do I tell if it's structural or geometric?

faq.q: How do I determine if a molecule can have E or Z isomers?
faq.a: You must have restricted rotation, usually due to a double bond or a ring structure. Each carbon attached to the double bond must have two different groups.
asks: Does every double bond mean E/Z?
What is the rule for E/Z naming?

faq.q: When counting isomers, do I need to worry about stereochemistry?
faq.a: Yes, you must consider all types, including structural and geometric isomers. Drawing them systematically prevents you from missing any unique arrangement.
asks: Is counting isomers just about the backbone?
Must I draw all possible stereoisomers?

faq.q: If I change the substituents, does it change the isomer count?
faq.a: Yes, changing substituents can create entirely new structural or geometric isomers. Always treat the new groups as unique when counting.
asks: Does adding a methyl group create a new isomer?
How does substitution affect isomer count?

faq.q: What is the priority rule for E/Z notation?
faq.a: You assign priorities based on the atomic number. The higher the atomic number, the higher the priority group.
asks: Is it just about the first atom?

facts: Isomers share the same molecular formula but differ in structure.
Structural isomers have different connectivity of atoms.
Geometric isomerism arises from restricted rotation, often across a double bond.
The E/Z system uses Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules for priority.

quiz.say: Given the formula $\text{C}4\text{H}8$, which of these structures represents a geometric isomer?

options.show: The one with a double bond and two different groups on each side.
options.say: The one with a double bond and two different groups on each side.

quiz.why: Geometric isomerism requires restricted rotation, which is typically found across a double bond, allowing for E or Z arrangements.

wrong.0: This is a structural isomer based on connectivity, not restricted rotation.
wrong.2: This is a structural isomer, but it does not necessarily show restricted rotation.
wrong.3: Cyclic structures are different types of isomers, but not specifically E/Z geometric isomers.

quiz.say: To correctly count all possible isomers for $\text{C}4\text{H}{10}$, what is the best method?

options.show: Drawing the first two isomers you think of.
options.say: Drawing the first two isomers you think of.

options.show: Systematic drawing based on carbon backbone length and branching.
options.say: Systematic drawing based on carbon backbone length and branching.

options.show: Only counting the longest straight chain.
options.say: Only counting the longest straight chain.

options.show: Counting only the number of carbons.
options.say: Counting only the number of carbons.

quiz.why: Systematic drawing ensures you account for every unique arrangement without repetition or omission.

wrong.0: This is unreliable and highly likely to miss other possible arrangements.
wrong.2: This ignores all possible branched structures that share the same formula.
wrong.3: The formula $ ext{C}4 ext{H}{10}$ defines the total atoms, not just the count of carbons.

quiz.say: If a molecule has the formula $\text{C}2\text{H}4$, what is the most stable structure?
quiz.why: Ethene is the simplest alkene derived from two carbons, $\text{C}2\text{H}4$, which is the most common stable arrangement.

wrong.0: Ethane has the formula $ ext{C}2 ext{H}6$, not $ ext{C}2 ext{H}4$.
wrong.1: Cyclopropane has the formula $ ext{C}3 ext{H}6$, not $ ext{C}2 ext{H}4$.
wrong.2: This compound has a different functional group and a different formula.
